text: {"rules":[{"jurisdiction":"CA","level":"state","category":"just_cause_eviction","status":"in_force","title":"California Tenant Protection Act: just cause required to terminate tenancies","requirement":"After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months (or 24 months if an additional adult tenant was added before an existing tenant reached 24 months), the owner may not terminate the tenancy without just cause stated in the written termination notice. At-fault just causes include nonpayment of rent, breach of a material lease term, nuisance, waste, refusal to sign a lease extension, criminal activity, unauthorized subletting, refusal of lawful entry, unlawful use, and failure to vacate after termination or after giving notice. No-fault just causes include owner or family move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, compliance with a government or court order or local ordinance, and demolition or substantial remodel. Curable violations require a notice to cure before a three-day notice to quit. For no-fault terminations the owner must give relocation assistance equal to one month's rent within 15 calendar days of service of the notice, or waive the final month's rent. The notice must state the tenant's right to this. Owner move-in requires occupancy within 90 days for at least 12 months, and tenants get re-rental rights if the demolition or remodel is not carried out. Owners must give tenants a notice about these protections.
